transcript:
Header: 2025-05-09 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~72m | Recording ID: ff-20250509-nbf-01
Attendees: Jordan Klein (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Cho (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Northbridge Head of AI), Ellen Park (ML Platform), Samir Patel (SRE), Leah Ortiz (PM), Dana Li (Security)

[00:00] Jordan: ok everyone thanks for hopping on, the goal today is very practical, run through an apples-to-apples benchmark plan we can actually execute in your environment, and highlight gotchas like kv cache warm states, batching, and quantization differences.
[01:12] Marco: sounds good. high level we want to validate latency and cost for our 13B and 70B offline assistants, and make sure private deployment meets our residency and encryption constraints.
[02:05] Priya: great, quick framing — by "apples-to-apples" we mean same model weights, same tokenizer, identical seed/prompt inputs, same decoding params (temp/stop/beam), same hardware family if possible, and same pre/post-processing. also we capture both p50/p95/p99 tail latency and tokens/sec for throughput.
[03:20] Ellen: can you remind us how you handle KV cache for multi-turn? we see big swings in latency when context grows. is that a runtime thing or our workload?
[04:05] Priya: good question. runtime-wise, Redwood's serving runtime keeps KV cache in GPU memory keyed by conversation id; warm cache lookups are O(1) essentially and avoid recomputing prefix. but cache eviction policies, shard placement, and networked kv (for Private in VPC) can add variance. also cold start — first request to a new convo or after a reload — will be slower. we need to explicitly test warm vs cold sequences.
[05:30] Samir: when you say networked kv in VPC, do you mean a separate service? that adds latency to every step right?
[06:10] Alex: in Private setups there are two patterns: colocated KV in the same pod (best latency) or a managed remote KV store over the internal network (more flexible but higher tail). for apples-to-apples we suggest testing both patterns if you plan to use remote KV.
[07:02] Marco: ok noted. prompt sets — what's a good canonical set? we have short transactional prompts, long-form analysis prompts, and multi-turn flows. which ratio should we use?
[07:45] Priya: the recommended approach is to create slices: 40% short (<=64 tokens), 40% medium (65-512 tokens), 20% long (>512 tokens). also include multi-turn sequences where you feed previously generated tokens back in to exercise KV. we will give you a template CSV with columns: prompt_id, category, tokens_estimate, conversation_length, expected_behavior.
[09:12] Leah: and what about sampling? do we randomize prompts per virtual user or stick to fixed sequences to control variance?
[09:40] Priya: for latency tests keep deterministic sequences per connection to measure tail. for throughput stress runs randomize across the slice to simulate production mix. include a separate steady-state run and a ramp test to observe autoscaling and warmup.
[11:00] Jordan: load generation — customers often use Locust or Vegeta; we maintain a dockerized harness that wraps Locust and our SDK so it can hit both hosted and private endpoints with identical client behavior. will share the repo.
[12:28] Marco: any advice on headers/timeouts/retries to make it fair vs e.g., OpenAI hosted APIs?
[13:05] Priya: align client timeouts to your SLOs — e.g., 3s for p50 target, 10s for tail. disable client-side retries during latency tail measurement; otherwise retries obscure actual service tail. also standardize chunked streaming vs non-streaming — streaming adds TTFB measurement and can change p95. pick the output mode you care about.
[14:45] Ellen: quantization — we plan to test int8 and fp16. what deltas should we expect and how to run?
[15:25] Alex: quantization tradeoffs depend on model family. expect ~1.5x-3x throughput improvement with int8 on many encoder-decoder and decoder-only models and 5-15% quality drop in some categories. do a quality regression harness (we recommend 200 human-evaluated prompts across slices). our harness can run accuracy metrics (ROUGE/BLEU/embedding-similarity) as part of the run.
[16:48] Marco: do you control kernel selection? our infra team wants to know if Triton or custom kernels are in play.
[17:20] Priya: runtime picks kernels by heuristics — sequence length, batch size, and device. in Redwood Dedicated/Private we surface a kernel profile. for apples-to-apples, pin the kernel stack: same CUDA version, cudnn/cutlass, and the same runtime commit. otherwise micro-ops differ.
[18:55] Samir: are there CPU affinity or numa settings customers typically miss?
[19:30] Alex: yes, pinning the worker threads and isolating NIC interrupts matters. For on-prem tests we recommend isolating one CPU socket per GPU and disabling hyperthreading for cleaner runs. document these env settings in the harness so runs are reproducible.
[21:04] Jordan: let's talk metrics — we capture p50/p95/p99 latency, TTFB (time to first token), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory footprint, and energy if available. also measure cold-start time for model load and for KV misses.
[22:18] Ellen: how to measure warm vs cold KV systematically?
[22:45] Priya: two test types: (1) cold sequence: create new conversation id each request to force fresh KV; (2) warm sequence: reuse same conv id and pre-warm the cache with N requests, then measure subsequent latencies. vary the number of warm keys and content size. include eviction tests by running high cardinality of conv ids.
[24:12] Marco: what about batching? we expect to use small batches for low latency but larger batches for cost efficiency. how do we compare fairly?
[24:50] Alex: define target SLO bucket — e.g., sub-200ms median for assistant. run a family of runs sweeping batch size [1,2,4,8,16] and capture latency distributions. compute cost-per-token at each point by dividing run cost by tokens generated. include client-side batching vs server-side continuous batching behavior. in continuous batching, prefix cache reduces token compute so cost math differs.
[26:43] Leah: you mentioned server-side continuous batching — is it deterministic? sometimes we see higher variance due to batching windows.
[27:10] Priya: continuous batching uses a latency budget where requests wait up to X ms for a batch to fill. set that budget in the harness and test multiple values. capture batch composition histograms. for apples-to-apples, synchronize budgets across platforms (e.g., 5ms, 10ms, 50ms).
[28:55] Marco: RPS vs concurrency — how to pick load profiles?
[29:20] Jordan: run two profiles: steady concurrency (fixed number of parallel connections with pipelined requests) and steady RPS (requests per second). RPS tests reveal how autoscaling behaves; concurrency tests show tail effects under constant pressure. both are useful.
[31:00] Dana (Security): quick question on Private deployment and encryption — do you require outbound connections to Redwood control plane? we need to keep traffic zero egress if possible.
[31:35] Priya: Redwood Private can be deployed with a closed control plane; minimal egress required only for optional telemetry. for testing we can run the runtime fully in your VPC. we'll send an onboarding doc listing ports and KMS integration patterns.
[33:05] Ellen: any gotchas with tokenization mismatch between frameworks?
[33:40] Alex: yes — make sure you use identical tokenizer binary and version; whitespace handling and special tokens can shift token counts which in turn affects batching and costs. the harness will verify token counts per prompt.
[35:10] Marco: how to do apples-to-apples across cloud providers when hardware differs? we can't provision identical GPUs everywhere.
[35:45] Priya: two options: (A) normalize per-GPU performance by reporting throughput per GPU rather than system throughput; (B) choose representative GPU families and run on each with the same driver/kernel stack where possible. include cost normalization (cost per token) in the comparison. note vendor-specific kernel optimizations can create differences so be explicit about CPU/GPU microsetup.
[37:20] Samir: for on-prem we'll probably run with mixed batch sizes and some GPUs using MIG. does that break comparability?
[37:50] Alex: MIG complicates latency profiles; if you intend to use MIG in production, include MIG runs. otherwise keep MIG off for baseline parity. document MIG config as metadata for each run.
[39:12] Leah: what about failure modes — OOMs and retries?
[39:40] Priya: include error rate and recovery time metrics: percent OOM, percent 5xx, time-to-recover (scale-up), and trace IDs to reproduce. set client behavior to surface raw errors in the run logs rather than hiding them.
[41:05] Jordan: on the quality evaluation for quantized models — we recommend automated embedding-similarity thresholds plus spot human eval. we'll provide a 200-case gold set and a template for rubric.
[42:30] Marco: do you have a recommended baseline run order?
[42:50] Priya: yes: (1) baseline host: run unquantized fp16 single-tenant run single-threaded to get raw numbers; (2) cold vs warm KV; (3) batch sweep; (4) quantized variants; (5) mixed traffic; (6) failure injection and recovery; (7) long-run steady-state to measure drift.
[44:12] Ellen: how long should each run be? 10 minutes? 30?
[44:30] Alex: for p95 stability aim for at least 10 minutes steady-state, ideally 30 minutes for tail stability and autoscaling. cold-start tests are shorter — a few iterations.
[45:55] Marco: earlier you mentioned capture of kernel profiles — can you include the runtime commit hash and kernel logs in the artifact?
[46:20] Priya: yes we'll add runtime commit, CUDA/cudnn versions, kernel selection logs, and environment snapshot to the harness artifact.
[47:48] Dana: security again — will you share the harness code? we need code review for egress and secrets handling.
[48:10] Jordan: yes we will open the repo and provide a read-only sso link and a minimal docker image. secrets are loaded from your vault; the harness supports injecting creds via environment vars and does not store them.
[49:55] Marco: timing wise when can we run the on-prem harness?
[50:20] Jordan: if we get the prompt CSV and VPC access by 5/13, we can schedule engineers to run the harness with you week of 5/19.
[51:35] Priya: final note on apples-to-apples: capture raw token-level logs and request IDs so we can replay any sample to check model output differences. small differences in tokenization or decoding seeds create divergence.
[52:50] Ellen: one last thing — cost math, can you provide a simple cost-per-100k-token calc under different batch/quantization combos?
[53:20] Alex: yes we'll produce a spreadsheet template: rows are runs, cols are p50/p95/p99, tokens generated, GPU-hours, infra cost, and normalized cost per 100k tokens.
[54:33] Jordan: ok let's recap actions and owners — Priya will push harness, Marco will share prompts, Samir provi will give VPC creds, Jordan will send SOC2 deck and onboarding doc. date for follow up run week of 5/19.
[55:12] Marco: agreed. thanks everyone.
[56:00] [end of recording — some chatter about calendars and links]

Artifacts mentioned: - GH repo: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmark-harness (will share tag) - prompt template CSV (attached in follow-up) - quantization config matrix (Redwood to send) - SOC2 + security onboarding doc (Jordan)
